top_choice_rationale: P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) combines new data, credible quasi-experimental designs and an explanatory account of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets. That is the data-plus-framework combination I value. The work is more than a decade old and has been re-estimated and challenged by many independent users, which I count as maturity. The three-name set follows the authorship of the China-shock papers, and the citation is limited to the empirical evidence, so it makes no priority claim for the task framework. I accept that persistence and shift-share identification are still debated and that the task-framework originators are uncredited. I also accept that P001 has cleaner two-name attribution and a framework that has been absorbed for longer, and I rank it second as a strong, defensible alternative. P003 follows because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are left out of the credited set and the contribution rests heavily on one 2003 paper, although it has dense empirical support. An award on any of the three is preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; B018 is close to my own field of labour economics, which I disclose as field proximity. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any proposal in the slate, and I have no documented tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Helpman, Grossman or Melitz.
